clue.text: Kill and fight for somewhere to keep a substance for snorting

definitions.text: somewhere to keep a substance for snorting

parts.note: to snuff someone out is to kill them
to box is to fight with fists

explanation.surface: A violent pair of verbs seemingly leading to a hiding place for cocaine.
explanation.definitionFit: Snuff is powdered tobacco taken up the nose, and its small lidded container has a dedicated name.

clue.text: Brenda's residence lacks the soothing ointment for one type of sex

indicators.note: something that lacks a part has had it taken away, so these letters drop out

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose Scottish home is Balmoral
balm is a soothing ointment

explanation.surface: The Queen's castle running out of soothing cream, a strange preface to sex.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II; Balmoral is her castle in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral sex is one variety of sexual activity, so the adjective names the type.

clue.text: Intelligentsia tured on by amphetamine artist — it's sick

parts.note: turned on (as printed, missing an n) means lit, like a lamp
E is slang for ecstasy, an amphetamine-type drug
RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist

indicators.note: sick means thrown up, and in a down clue thrown up means read upwards

parts.note: the word it, with the 's acting as a link

explanation.surface: Intellectuals getting high on speed and art until it makes them ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'tured' is a slip for 'turned'. In a down clue, 'sick' (thrown up) sends the last piece upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The literati are the educated, literary class, a near synonym for the intelligentsia.

clue.text: Do this up and drug yourself

definitions.text: Do this up and drug yourself

parts.words: Do this up and drug yourself
parts.note: the phrasal verb formed with up means to inject a drug

explanation.walkthrough: 'Do this up' reads like fastening clothing, but the verb wanted joins 'up' to make the slang for injecting drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot up is drug slang for injecting heroin or similar into a vein.

clue.text: Edwina's 150 turns — a dangerous power source as it was once known

definitions.text: a dangerous power source as it was once known

indicators.note: turns means these letters revolve into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
CL is 150 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Edwina Currie spinning around, with a dig at nuclear power.
explanation.walkthrough: Edwina Currie was a Conservative MP, a Private Eye target.
explanation.definitionFit: Windscale was the earlier name of the Sellafield nuclear site in Cumbria, scene of a 1957 reactor fire.

clue.text: Bill has a crazy hep exterior of a native American

indicators.note: the shuffled letters form an exterior, wrapping round the account
crazy means the letters of hep go wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
AC is short for account, which is a bill

explanation.surface: A man named Bill with a mad, hip outer shell turns out to be a Native American.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apache are a group of Native American peoples of the south-western United States.

clue.text: Reprimand makes you throw up on getting engaged

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the first part sits above the second
in a down clue, up means the word for throw is read from the bottom

parts.note: to lob is to throw
gears or parts locking are engaging with each other

explanation.surface: A telling-off so bad it makes you vomit just as you get engaged to be married.
explanation.walkthrough: A bollocking is British slang for a severe telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang noun means a harsh scolding, so it stands for a reprimand.

clue.text: "Vera screwed by politician", put rather differently

indicators.note: screwed means twisted, so the name's letters are turned into another order

parts.note: taken as written
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A tabloid line about a woman named Vera and a politician, reworded.
explanation.definitionFit: To revamp something is to rework or revise it, presenting it in a new form.

clue.text: Name given by Brenda to heart-throb rather like Mr Bean

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, whose royal cipher is ER
a dish is an attractive person

explanation.surface: The Queen bestowing a nickname on a pin-up who resembles Mr Bean.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bean is Rowan Atkinson's awkward comic character.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Bean is a socially inept, geeky figure, and the suffix -ish makes the adjective mean somewhat like that.

clue.text: Burst in on oldie MP getting changed

indicators.note: getting changed means these letters are altered into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone barging in on an elderly MP while he is changing clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that implodes collapses violently inwards, which is bursting in.

clue.text: Wrong cover for Jeffrey Archer's type of fiction?

parts.note: false means wrong
a hood is a head covering

explanation.surface: A misleading book jacket for a bestselling novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was convicted of perjury in 2001, so his 'fiction' was lying in court.
explanation.definitionFit: A falsehood is a lie, which the question mark makes a type of fiction for a man who told lies under oath.

clue.text: TV celeb, Dicky, in C&A

indicators.note: in puts the poorly word inside the shop's name

parts.note: the letters of the high-street clothing chain
dicky is British slang for unwell or shaky, which is ill

explanation.surface: A television star feeling poorly while out shopping at a chain store.
explanation.walkthrough: C&A was a well-known British high-street clothing chain; dicky, as in a dicky heart, means unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Cilla Black was a famous British singer and television presenter, known by her first name.

clue.text: Fast food: obese dirty old man's habit?

parts.note: big means fat
the stereotypical flasher wears a mac, short for mackintosh raincoat

explanation.surface: A burger and an unpleasant man's regular clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'dirty old man in a mac' is a British stereotype of a flasher; a mac is a raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: The Big Mac is McDonald's famous hamburger, the archetype of fast food.

clue.text: Gnome TV broadcast includes Brenda and new Labour ministers

indicators.note: includes means the shuffled letters hold the Queen and new inside
broadcast means scattered, so these letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen, whose royal cipher is ER

explanation.surface: Private Eye's proprietor Lord Gnome launching a TV channel featuring the Queen and the new cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Gnome is Private Eye's fictional proprietor.
explanation.definitionFit: In 2000 Labour formed the government, the body of ministers running the country.

clue.text: Bonk and peak with bottle-top

parts.note: bonk and screw are both slang for having sex
a peaked hat is a cap, and the peak names it

explanation.surface: Sex at the summit with a bottle in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw cap is the threaded lid that closes a bottle, a common type of bottle closure.

clue.text: Daily, Labour's leader gets one over Brown — the impostor!

parts.note: a daily is a cleaner, also called a char or charwoman

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Labour, picked out by leader
a means one
tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about Labour's leader standing over Gordon Brown and branding him a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: Daily and char are both British words for a cleaning lady; Brown suggests Gordon Brown, then Chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlatan is a fraud who claims skills he lacks, so a pretender or impostor.

clue.text: Violet has sex with divine politician, with kinky aid, after kisses and "activities down under"

definitions.note: the games held in Australia, a plural word standing for one event

indicators.note: the rest comes after the kisses, so they lead

parts.note: XX at the end of a letter are kisses
Vi is the short form of the name Violet
it is a coy word for sex
holy means divine
MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so these letters are bent into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid tale of Violet, a pious MP and some sexual activities down under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Activities down under' reads as sexual innuendo; it means the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games, numbered the twenty-seventh Olympiad.
explanation.definitionFit: The 2000 Summer Olympics were held in Sydney, Australia, and are officially the Games of the XXVII Olympiad.

clue.text: Go soft and fluff nuclear accident

parts.note: to melt is to soften
down is soft fluffy feathers

explanation.surface: Softening and fluff sound gentle, then comes a nuclear disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A meltdown is when a reactor's core overheats and melts, a severe nuclear accident.

clue.text: Hanging around not having an erection

definitions.meaning: second meaning: hanging limp, as a flaccid penis does

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like loitering; the second half gives the rude sense of something hanging limply.
explanation.definitionFit: The participle describes anything suspended loosely, which covers both loose hanging and a limp member.

clue.text: One way to present statistics from Blair primarily: sly ingenuity

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of Blair, picked out by primarily
arch means slyly knowing
art means skill or ingenuity

explanation.surface: A jibe that Tony Blair's figures come from cunning spin.
explanation.definitionFit: A bar chart shows data as bars of differing lengths, a common graph format for numbers.

clue.text: Biro and old records deployed by strong-arm types?

parts.note: Bic is a brand of ballpoint pen, like a Biro
EPs are extended-play records, now old-fashioned

explanation.surface: Thugs using a pen and a stack of vinyl as weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: Biro is the British everyday name for a ballpoint pen.
explanation.definitionFit: The biceps are upper-arm muscles, so playfully they are the types that make an arm strong.

clue.text: Stir no longer produced by hospital head

definitions.note: stir is slang for prison; this one closed in 2000

parts.note: H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital
block is slang for the head, as in knock someone's block off

explanation.surface: A hospital chief making something no longer move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' looks like a verb, but it is the slang for prison. The H-Blocks of the Maze prison in Northern Ireland were emptied in 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: The H-Blocks were the Maze prison's H-shaped cell buildings, which stopped being a jail in 2000.

clue.text: Political catchphrase from 'Hard Work' article

parts.note: a slog is hard work
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A political slogan lifted from an essay called 'Hard Work'.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan is a short memorable phrase used in political campaigns and advertising.

clue.text: Sounds like a means of passing on casual wear

indicators.note: sounds like means the word is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: genes are how traits are passed on to offspring

explanation.surface: Handing down comfortable clothing, as if hand-me-downs.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeans are denim trousers, the classic informal clothing.

clue.text: Beast humped, reached orgasm and left

parts.note: came is slang for reached orgasm

explanation.surface: A crude tale of a quick encounter: humped, climaxed, and walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humped' looks like a crude verb, but it describes the animal's back.
explanation.definitionFit: The camel is the animal famous for the hump or humps on its back.

clue.text: Like a story about Nato deal involving Chechnya's leader?

indicators.note: involving means the shuffled letters wrap round the letter added
about means the letters are moved around

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Chechnya, picked out by leader

explanation.surface: A report about a Nato deal involving the Chechen leader, which sounds like hearsay.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal means based on personal accounts or anecdotes, so story-like rather than proven.

clue.text: Send up American publication

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: to emit is to send out

explanation.surface: A satirical send-up of a US magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send up' looks like mockery, but it splits: send is the word, up turns it.
explanation.definitionFit: Time is a long-running weekly news magazine published in the United States.

clue.text: Pot and crack (top grade), the universal fix

parts.note: a pan is a cooking pot
a crack player is an ace, an expert
A is the top grade in exams

explanation.surface: Cannabis and crack cocaine sold as the drug that fixes everything.
explanation.definitionFit: A panacea is a supposed remedy for all ills, a cure-all.

clue.text: Hack sticking point into sensitive male

indicators.note: sticking means the compass point is pushed into the man
into says the point goes inside the other word

parts.note: a new man is a caring, sensitive modern man
S is south, a compass point

explanation.surface: A violent stabbing of a gentle, caring man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' looks like a verb to go with sticking a point in; it is a noun, a journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Hack is slang for a journalist, and a newsman is a reporter.
